recentItems.title: Venice Film Fest director defends lack of women directors in competition
recentItems.description:
(1 Sep 2026) 

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Venice, Italy - 1 September 2026
1. Various shots Alberto Barbera speaking with reporters
2. SOUNDBITE (English) Alberto Barbera, artistic director, Venice International Film Festival:
"We received a lot of submissions, as you know. Most of the things that we saw during the long selection process were dealing about contemporary problems. They are really ready to take the risk to deal with strong subject matters and without hiding themselves from the contemporary world. So we didn't have a choice. I mean, most of the beautiful films that we selected are dealing with this kind of problem. We have a space open to everybody for discussion, for confrontation. Everybody is completely free to express themselves. And in a way, I'm really happy that this kind of film could help the viewers, the critics, everybody, to have a better understanding of what is going on in our contemporary, difficult world."
3. Medium shot Alberto Barbera speaking with reporter
4. SOUNDBITE (English) Alberto Barbera, artistic director, Venice International Film Festival - on the lack of women directors in competition at this year's festival:
"The problem is that we saw a lot of films by women which are interesting. We put a lot of films in the sidebar section of the festival. But you couldn't find films so strong or strong enough to compete with other films in the main competition. But again, nobody can have doubts about our attitude towards these kinds of problems. We are on the side of women in their battle."
5. Wide shot Alberto Barbera speaking with reporter
6. SOUNDBITE (English) Alberto Barbera, artistic director, Venice International Film Festival:
"I'm sure there will be quite a number of films that are in Venice that will do the campaign for the Oscar, starting from the opening films, "Ink" by Danny Boyle, the new film by Martin McDonagh, of course, the film by Lee Chang-dong, maybe Florian Zeller's "Bunker" with Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz. There will be a lot of films, for sure."
7. Wide shot Alberto Barbera speaking with reporter
8. SOUNDBITE (English) Alberto Barbera, artistic director, Venice International Film Festival - on George Clooney getting lifetime achievement award:
"He's a good friend of the festival. He started to come at the end of the '90s and he came back many, many times. We decided to give him a Golden Lion because in a way he suffers from his own image, you know, the seductive man, an image of beauty and so on. And sometimes people forget that he is a great actor, one of the greatest actors at the moment, and a great filmmaker, a great director. So, I mean, it's a way to underline this thing."
9. Wide shot Alberto Barbera speaking with reporter

STORYLINE:
Alberto Barbera, artistic director of the Venice International Film Festival, has been talking about the sometimes controversial line-up the day before the event.

The festival kicks off on Wednesday and runs through Sept. 12, when the awards will be announced. The opening night film is Danny Boyle’s “Ink,” an adaptation of the acclaimed stage play about the early years of Rupert Murdoch — played by Guy Pearce — and his acquisition of the daily newspaper The Sun. Jack O’Connell and Claire Foy also star.

Barbera told The Associated Press that the 21 films in competition for the top prize, the Golden Lion, tackle difficult subjects head on.

"They are really ready to take the risk to deal with strong subject matters and without hiding themselves from the contemporary world," he said.

recentItems.title: Some schools in Jerusalem suspend classes as West Bank staff entry permits not renewed by Israel
recentItems.description:
(1 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Jerusalem – 1 September 2026
1. Wide of closed entrance to school
2. Close up of sign reading (English) “St. George’s School Est. 1899”
3. Close up of closed door
4. Interior of empty classroom
5. Mid of paper on wall reading (English) “Welcome to school 2026/2027”
6. Exterior pan right of empty playgrounds
7. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Richard Zananiri, General Director of Saint George’s school in Jerusalem:
“The day that we have been eagerly waiting for; the opening of the school year and the return of life, with the students, to these completely empty yards. Of course, we were shocked and stunned that a large number of female teachers, male teachers, male employees, and female employees from a large number of Jerusalem schools did not receive permits. These permits, of course, are the ones given to our people in the West Bank in order to reach the schools.”
8. Teacher entering class 
9. Teacher organizing tables in empty classroom 
10. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Richard Zananiri, General Director of Saint George’s school in Jerusalem:
“Therefore, today our position was taken despite the fact that we carry a message of peace, a message of love, a message of justice. We prepare our students only for universities. Today, we are surprised that we do not have permits, and specifically, we did not have permits for the employees; the employees who are responsible for maintenance, responsible for cleaning, responsible for security; whom I consider more important than me as a school principal. He is more important than me in this school.”
11. Various of empty classrooms
12. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Richard Zananiri, General Director of Saint George’s school in Jerusalem:
“We have a large number affected by this suspension of classes, around 26,000 to 28,000 students who are not in the schools. The female and male teachers who have permits are all here, working at the school, waiting, God willing, for life to return to normal and God willing, this matter will end today before tomorrow.”
13. Mid of Zananiri talking to teacher
14. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Richard Zananiri, general director of Saint George’s school in Jerusalem:
"Today, you have many specializations that are missing; you have a very large shortage. We have a shortage of around 146 classrooms in Jerusalem. Therefore, we always have a shortage of teachers. We are talking about 25 to 30 percent of our teachers being from the West Bank. Tomorrow, if I fall into this problem, where am I going to get a teacher from? Now, there are alternatives for some who may be in Jerusalem, but they cannot cover all the needs. They cannot cover all the specializations that exist. Therefore, we have no choice except to have the issue of West Bank teachers.”
15. Exterior of school
STORYLINE:
Private schools in Jerusalem suspended classes Tuesday after entry permits for dozens of teachers and staff from the West Bank were not renewed, preventing them from reaching their workplaces as the new school year began.

The Christian Schools in Jerusalem said entry permits for more than 70 teachers and staff working in educational, administrative, health and support roles had not been renewed. The group said classes would remain suspended until the permits are renewed and staff are able to return to their schools.

At Saint George’s School in Jerusalem, Richard Zananiri, the school’s general director, said teachers who had permits were at the school Tuesday, waiting for classes to resume.



He said schools face shortages of teachers and certain specializations and rely on teachers from the West Bank.

recentItems.title: Meet descendants of apartheid era wolves who can never leave their sanctuary
recentItems.description:
(1 Sep 2026) 
ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Hartbeespoort, South Africa - 24 July 2026

1. Wide of wolves in sanctuary
2. Mid of wolf named Lily standing by a fence
3. Close of wolves by a fenced area in the sanctuary
4. Wide of Ronnie Austen, Co-owner All Hearts Foundation, playing with one of the wolves
5. SOUNDBITE (English) Ronnie Austen, Co-owner All Hearts Foundation:
"We take care of about 60 wolves. We've got a couple of hybrids in between the wolves, so you're looking at about 67, somewhere around there of the wolves. Bear in mind these wolves eat a lot of raw they only eat raw. There's the odd few that we'll give a couple of dog food, dog pellets to which is kibble, but their main diet is raw. So we go through about 4.5 to 6 tonnes of chicken in a monthly period and then when it comes to red meat, we'll get anything from like say two to three cows in a month sometimes.”

6. Wide of wolves looking out from the fence 
7. Mid of a Austen walking towards semi-tame wolves in a fenced area
8. Close of a wolf behind a chain-link fence in a sanctuary 
9. SOUNDBITE (English) Ronnie Austen, Co-owner All Hearts Foundation:
"Us as humans have brought them into our country and they can't be released, they can't be released into our wild.  If you had to take one of these animals and take it back to its original country and try to release it, I don't think that would work either. Why? Because the majority of the wolves that are at our facility, or should I say all of the wolves at our facility, were all hand raised by humans so they weren't young and lived in the wild, if I can put it like that."

10. Wide of wolf walking towards camera 
11. Wide of wolf behind a chain-link fence in the sanctuary

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Cape Town, South Africa - 4 August 2026

12. SOUNDBITE (English) Sandra Swart, Professor, Chair of the Department of History at Stellenbosch University:
"Once the military project disappeared, there was no obvious institutional role for these animals. Some ended up in private hands, some ended up in the exotic animal trade and some became deeply unwanted, because a wolf hybrid is not a dog, as I've explained, and they found their way into sanctuaries that you've seen as well, but it's kind of a refuge for the living remnants of this old military experiment. So the wolves imported to South Africa to serve the machinery of apartheid security became the unwanted relics of that system."

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Hartbeespoort, South Africa - 24 July 2026

13. Mid of Lexi Austin, Founder of All Hearts Foundation, interacting with wolf through a fence
14. Close of wolf pushing its nose through fence
15. SOUNDBITE (English) Lexi Austen, Founder All Hearts foundation: 
“So all of our enclosures we have designed in such a way where they are offered the five freedoms. Wolves love swimming so every wolf camp has a swimming pool. We will often hang meat within the trees so that they can go and tug on the meat in the trees, and that's an enrichment activity, we allow big vast enclosure spaces so that they can dig the dens like they like to do in the wild, so we do our utmost best, but at the end of the day the reality is nothing will ever truly mimic the wild.”

16. Various of Ronnie Austen sitting with a wolves in an enclosure
17. Wide of a silhouetted wolf howling behind a fence at sunset
STORYLINE:
LEADIN:

A sanctuary in South Africa is taking care of wolves descended from animals imported by the repressive apartheid regime in the '70s.

They cannot be released into the wild as they are not native.

STORYLINE:

recentItems.title: China MOFA Highlights
recentItems.description:
(1 Sep 2026) 

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Beijing, China -  01 September 2026
Spokesperson: Guo Jiakun

1. Yesterday, the spokesperson provided an update on China’s disaster relief assistance to Nepal. What further support does China plan to provide for Nepal’s disaster relief efforts?

Providing emergency assistance to the disaster-hit areas in Nepal and engaging in international rescue cooperation is an important political decision made by China, reflecting our friendly ties with Nepal.
China’s second batch of relief supplies for Nepal is expected to be shipped today, including items urgently needed by Nepal such as drones, DNA testing equipment and reagents, water purification equipment, and lighting equipment. Chinese DNA testing experts will also head to the disaster-hit areas to assist Nepal in their operation. 
China will stand firmly with Nepal, join hands to overcome the difficult time as part of our efforts to carry forward the traditional friendship between neighboring countries through concrete actions.

2. While Nepal has let in many journalists to cover this devastating mudslide and their rescue efforts, why has China so far refused access to foreign journalists to the disaster zone on the Tibetan side? Secondly, do you have any further information about the Australian who has recently been found alive on the Tibet side? 

On your first question, the roads and communication are currently cut off in the disaster-hit areas, where the risk of secondary disasters remains high. The intense rescue efforts are being carried out in an intensive and orderly manner, and we will continue to release the latest information on the disaster situation and rescue operations.
Regarding your second question, as I said earlier, China is currently making every effort to search for and rescue missing persons, both Chinese nationals and foreign nationals. We are maintaining close communication with foreign diplomatic missions in China to jointly identify missing foreign nationals and handle follow-up matters. As for the specific case you mentioned, I will get back to you after checking with the relevant authorities for further details. 

3. Following the mudslide disaster in Nepal, has China shared information with Nepal? How frequently, hourly or daily?

China and Nepal have maintained good cooperation in meteorology, water resources, and disaster prevention and mitigation. Since the disaster, China and Nepal have maintained smooth communication on search and rescue operations, information sharing, and preventing secondary disasters. China has continuously provided Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data, conducted professional consultations, and issued relevant early warning information. 
China will continue to strongly support Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and strengthen cooperation in disaster prevention and mitigation so as to safeguard the common interests of the peoples of both countries.

4. As part of President Trump's new oil deal with Venezuela, the US oil company will take over several oil fields in Venezuela that were previously owned by Chinese companies. What is China’s response?

China has noted the relevant reports. China always maintains that relations between countries should be handled in accordance with the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, and that economic and trade cooperation between countries should follow the principles of equality and mutual benefit, and win-win cooperation.





7. The US and New Zealand have announced plans to jointly develop a deep-water port at a former military base in the Cook Islands. What is China’s comment?

recentItems.title: Traditional fans take center stage during heatwaves in Spain
recentItems.description:
(1 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Madrid, Spain — 29 August 2026
1. Various of people carrying hand fans on street
2. SOUNDBITE (Spanish) Macarena Gimenez, fan user: ++SOUNDBITE STARTS ON PREVIOUS SHOT AND IS OVERLAID BY SHOT 3++
“I came to Madrid, I am living in London. I use the fan because here in Madrid, it is very hot, with 35 degrees. I cannot take it anymore, I am not Spanish anymore, it seems.”
3. Various of people using fan
4. SOUNDBITE (Spanish) David Gonzalez, fan user: ++SOUNDBITE STARTS ON PREVIOUS SHOT AND IS OVERLAID BY SHOT 5-7++
“I like to use the fan because throughout the day with the heat it gives me fresh air, comfort. In the beginning I was a bit embarrassed because it is an item that is mostly linked with women, but I acknowledge it is useful and it makes my day better and in the end you leave your prejudices aside and today I take it everywhere.”
5. People using fan

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Madrid, Spain — 25 August 2026
6. Wide of shop window displaying fans
7. Tourist going through fan selection
8. Interior of traditional fan shop
9. SOUNDBITE (Spanish) Javier Llerandi, Casa de Diego shop owner: ++SOUNDBITE STARTS ON PREVIOUS SHOT AND IS OVERLAID BY SHOT 10++
“Our main customer is the Madrid resident. Followed by the national tourist and then the foreign tourist. We live off the heat, in the old days we only sold fans during summer. With increasing tourists in Madrid, we sell fans all year, and of course the heatwaves are good for this business.”
10. Various of customers looking at fans 
STORYLINE:
As successive heat waves in Western Europe pushed temperatures this summer to punishing levels, the accessory, the traditional folding hand fan, or abanico, has become an essential, embraced by young and old from Spain and elsewhere. 

On a recent August day, 20-year-old Ana Feliu blocked the sun with a paper abanico she was gifted during a Valencian festival. 

She carries it everywhere she goes in the summer — in equal parts for its ability to cool her down and to shield herself from the sun.

“This one is my favorite, but I have many,” she told The Associated Press near Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square.

Also fanning himself was David González, whose abanico featured pinks, purples and reds.

“At first, I felt a little self-conscious, because it’s something that’s mainly associated with women, but I have to admit it serves a purpose — and it brightens my day,” said González, 53.

The abanico has a rich history, arriving in Europe through Portuguese trade with Asia in the 15th century.

As early as the mid-17th century, the Spanish painter Diego Velázquez made his enigmatic "The Lady with a Fan," in which a woman in a black dress poses with what appears to be a delicate abanico made from wood.

By the 19th century, it was widely used by Spain's aristocracy. 

As the fans grew fashionable in European courts, Spain developed a taste and industry of its own. 

Madrid became an important center of production, and by the 18th century, Valencia had emerged as the Spanish fan-making capital.

Today, specialty shops like Casa de Diego in Madrid and kiosks selling cheap plastic fans report strong sales amid punishing heat.

In crowded subway cars and sun-drenched plazas, an old-fashioned accessory in Spain has been everywhere thanks to the blistering summer heat.

Small enough to fit into a purse, the traditional Spanish folding hand fan, or abanico, snaps open into a semicircle and is light enough to use with one hand. 

With little more than a flick of the wrist, it creates a surprisingly strong breeze.

recentItems.title: Search and rescue efforts continue following last week's catastrophic flooding as death toll in Nepa
recentItems.description:
(1 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Nuwakot District, Nepal - 1 September 2026
1. Zoom out of helicopter landing
2. Wide of people carrying belongings disembarking helicopter 
3. Various of military personnel carrying supplies and loading up helicopters
4. Various of helicopter, military personnel carrying supplies walking by
5. Wide of helicopter taking off
STORYLINE:
The death toll from catastrophic flooding in Nepal and China rose over 1,000 on Tuesday, authorities said, as rescue teams worked to reach communities cut off by the disaster.

Nepal’s disaster agency said Tuesday that 987 deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreigners. Chinese authorities, in their latest update on Sunday, reported 16 deaths and 546 people still missing, including 261 foreigners.

At least 11,814 people have been rescued so far, according to Nepalese authorities. Emergency crews have been using helicopters and other aircraft to reach stranded communities in areas where roads and bridges have been destroyed by the flooding and landslides.

The Aug. 26 disaster began with a chain of events high in the Himalayas. A glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.

Authorities are still searching for thousands of people who remain unaccounted for on Tuesday. Rescue teams are also working to provide assistance to survivors in areas where roads and other transportation routes have been damaged or cut off.

For rescuers, the immediate priority remains finding at least 900 workers who are missing from 12 hydropower projects damaged by the flash floods, about 500 of whom are believed to be trapped inside tunnels.

AP video shot by Rishi Lekhi

recentItems.title: Thailand's Pattaya anticipates USS Abraham Lincoln visit following its Middle East deployment
recentItems.description:
(1 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Pattaya, Thailand - 31 August 2026
1. Various from scenic overlook of Pattaya
2. Wide of Poramet Ngampichet, mayor of Pattaya
3. SOUNDBITE (Thai) Poramet Ngampichet, Mayor of Pattaya:
"The conflict in the Middle East has caused gas prices to soar, and the costs of traveling overseas have also increased. Therefore, the number of tourists has declined worldwide. So, this visit of the U.S. troops will partly help distribute income in a span of five days that they will spend in Pattaya."
4. Various of Pattaya beach
5. SOUNDBITE (Thai) Poramet Ngampichet, mayor of Pattaya:
"For Pattaya to be seen as an important vacation spot is something that we have aimed for, and we welcome more visits of the troops in the future, whether for a drill or a vacation, before they go back to the U.S."

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Pattaya, Thailand - 1 September 2026
6. Various of banner welcoming U.S. service members reading (English): "Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service."
7. SOUNDBITE (Thai) Bualuang Ponok, bar employee:
"They said 5,000 people will come here, but how many will reach us? There will be shuttle service taking them to other places, like Sattahip or Bangkok. It's really up to them."

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Pattaya, Thailand - 31 August 2026
8. Various of Pattaya's famous Walking Street
STORYLINE:
Thousands of US service members are about to descend on Thailand, as the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier makes a port call near the coastal city of Pattaya, known for its beaches and nightlife.

The Lincoln, as well as the destroyer the U.S.S Frank E. Petersen Jr., is expected to dock in eastern Thailand this week before heading back to the U.S. after a lengthy deployment in the Middle East as part of the U.S. war against Iran.

Concerns have grown about the Lincoln's lengthy deployment following reports of deteriorating mental health among the crew and shortages of supplies, including food and hygiene products.

Local business owners in Pattaya, feeling the tourism slump from the Iran war, are eager for the new arrivals and hope it will bolster sales. A local bar named after the famous mojito cocktail hung a banner welcoming American military personnel.

"The conflict in the Middle East has caused gas prices to soar, and the costs of traveling overseas have also increased," said Poramet Ngampichet, mayor of Pattaya. "Therefore, the number of tourists has declined worldwide. So, this visit of the U.S. troops will partly help distribute income in a span of five days that they will spend in Pattaya."

American officials estimate that a sailor could spend between $100 to $150 per day while in town, he said, calculating that this could generate about 100 million baht (approximately $3 million) throughout the visit.

"For Pattaya to be seen as an important vacation spot is something that we have aimed for, and we welcome more visits of the troops in the future, whether for a drill or a vacation, before they go back to the U.S.," he said.

Government officials are warning local businesses not to overcharge American sailors and there will be a greater police presence in popular areas along Pattaya Beach and the city’s Walking Street, Poramet said.

"They said 5,000 people will come here, but how many will reach us? There will be shuttle service taking them to other places, like Sattahip or Bangkok. It's really up to them," said Bualuang Ponok, a bar employee.

AP video shot by Anton L. Delgado

recentItems.title: Residents of Venezuela oil hub await impact of renewed operations, amid sweeping agreement with US
recentItems.description:
(1 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Cabimas, Venezuela - 31 August 2026
1. Various of oil pumps
2. Various of oil drilling infrastructure at Maracaibo Lake
3. SOUNDBITE (Spanish) Erwin Ayala, oil worker:
++PARTLY OVERLAID++
“They’re doing what they can—that’s what I’ve seen and quite clearly, since, as I told you, we don’t have the machinery or the technology to extract the oil we want. Right now, production is supposedly hovering around 700,000 to 800,000 barrels of oil. It’s not even reaching a million. Now, it’s estimated that once U.S. technology comes in, production will rise to at least 1.5 million barrels of oil. That’s what we’re hoping for—that those people will come in and create jobs. And that they open up the docks—at least where we’re not working—so we can have a smoother workflow. Because we’re working for minimum wage, and the minimum wage here in Venezuela is equivalent to 150 bolivars a month (less than $1), and that’s nothing to us—it’s what we’re making right now. And also we earn the “war bonus” which is $150 a month, and also we earn another bonus that is called a “month-end bonus” of $50. That’s all there is, and there’s this allowance to buy food that’s equivalent to $40 a month, but that’s nothing, here right now it’s nothing.”
4. Various of pumps working
5. Various of oil spill at shore in Maracaibo Lake
6. Various of oil drilling infrastructure at Maracaibo Lake
7. Mid of an oil tank
STORYLINE:
Residents in Cabimas, a historic petroleum hub on Lake Maracaibo, have long lived next to wells, pipelines and oil terminals, witnessing first hand the environmental fallout of Venezuela’s collapsing oil industry. 

Oil pumps move up and down between eroded homes, next to empty village-like streets under a scorching sun.  

An aging oil infrastructure stretches into Lake Maracaibo and crude stains its shoreline, troubling the livelihoods of hundreds of fishermen on the water of the lake that holds some of Venezuela’s massive oil reserves.

Residents of the historic oil city say they are seeing signs of renewed activity. Fisherman Carlos Rodriguez pointed to a pump he said had been inactive for more than 15 years but resumed operating about four months ago. Tankers can also be seen anchored offshore.

The renewed activity comes as the United States and Venezuela move forward with a sweeping oil agreement covering 17 fields. Venezuela’s government says the fields have a proven potential of 65 billion barrels and could attract more than $100 billion in investment.

But the agreement has not been made public, leaving unanswered questions about its financing, timetable and the companies that would participate. 

U.S. president Donald Trump calls the deal the “biggest oil deal ever.” 

Venezuelans wonder how–if at all– it will benefit them. In Cabimas, residents expressed a mixture of hope and resignation. Former and current oil workers have hope the deal will bring life back to a decaying industry that was once a thriving oil town.

For oil workers who once made one of the biggest incomes in the nation, the situation can be as dire as any public sector worker. 

“We’re working for minimum wage,” oil worker Erwin Ayala said, standing behind a small oil pump working on a quiet street next to his home.

He says the industry is slowly trying to get back on its feet but is aware it will take time. “We don’t have the machinery or the technology to extract the oil we want. Right now, production is supposedly hovering around 700,000 to 800,000 barrels of oil. It’s not even reaching a million,” he said.
